title: 20 shapes of pasta
hook: Every pasta shape is built for a sauce. Once you know the rule, you can order or cook in any Italian place without guessing.

items.name: Spaghetti
items.note: “little strings.” Tomato or olive-oil sauces.

items.name: Capellini
items.note: “angel hair,” the thinnest. Very light sauces or soup.

items.name: Linguine
items.note: “little tongues,” flat spaghetti. Seafood and pesto.

items.name: Bucatini
items.note: Thick spaghetti with a hole down the middle.

items.name: Fettuccine
items.note: Flat ribbons. Heavy cream sauces like Alfredo.

items.name: Pappardelle
items.note: Very wide ribbons. Thick meat sauce (ragù).

items.name: Penne
items.note: “quills,” cut on a slant. Sauce gets inside.

items.name: Rigatoni
items.note: Big ridged tubes. Chunky sauces and baking.

items.name: Ziti
items.note: Smooth tubes, cut straight. Baked ziti.

items.name: Macaroni
items.note: Small bent tubes. Mac and cheese.

items.name: Cannelloni
items.note: Large tubes you stuff, then bake.

items.name: Farfalle
items.note: “butterflies” (bow ties). Pasta salad.

items.name: Fusilli
items.note: Spirals that trap sauce in the grooves.

items.name: Orecchiette
items.note: “little ears.” Cups that hold vegetables.

items.name: Conchiglie
items.note: “shells.” Hold peas, cheese, sauce.

items.name: Radiatori
items.note: Shaped like old radiators. Thick sauces.

items.name: Orzo
items.note: Means “barley” — looks like rice. Soup.

items.name: Ravioli
items.note: Square pillows filled with cheese or meat.

items.name: Tortellini
items.note: Rings, filled. Often served in broth.

items.name: Lasagne
items.note: Wide sheets layered with sauce and cheese, baked.

facts: The rule: thin and smooth → light sauce. Wide or ridged → heavy sauce. Tiny → soup.
Dry pasta is just durum wheat (semolina) and water. Fresh pasta usually adds egg.
“Al dente” means “to the tooth”: cooked, but still a little firm in the middle.
The story that Marco Polo brought pasta from China is a myth. Pasta was in Italy before his trip, and China had its own noodles for thousands of years.
doIt: Go to the kitchen. Find every pasta box or bag. For each one, write its name and its cooking time from the package. Then write which sauce you would put on it, using the rule.

quiz.q: Which pasta is best for a thick meat sauce?
quiz.why: Wide ribbons are strong enough to carry a heavy sauce.
Orecchiette are little ears; spaghetti are little strings.

quiz.q: Which shape would you put in soup?
quiz.why: Tiny shapes fit on a spoon.

options: Cooked but still a little firm

title: Breads of the world
hook: Almost every culture has a bread. The big difference is what makes it rise — or whether it rises at all.

items.name: Baguette
items.note: France. Long, crisp crust, only flour, water, salt, yeast.

items.name: Challah
items.note: Jewish braided bread with egg, for Shabbat.

items.name: Bagel
items.note: Boiled first, then baked — that's the chewy skin.

items.name: Brioche
items.note: France. Rich with butter and eggs, almost a cake.

items.name: Focaccia
items.note: Italy. Flat, oily, dimpled with fingers.

items.name: Pita
items.note: Middle East. Steam puffs it into a pocket.

items.name: Naan
items.note: South Asia. Baked on the wall of a hot tandoor oven.

items.name: Sourdough
items.note: A “starter” of flour and water full of wild yeast and bacteria. The bacteria make it sour.

items.name: Rye / pumpernickel
items.note: Germany and Eastern Europe. Dark, dense, sour.

items.name: Injera
items.note: Ethiopia. Spongy, fermented teff flatbread. Also your plate and spoon.

items.name: Matzah
items.note: Flour and water baked fast, for Passover.

items.name: Tortilla
items.note: Mexico. Corn or wheat, cooked on a griddle.

items.name: Chapati / roti
items.note: India. Whole-wheat, cooked on a flat pan.

items.name: Irish soda bread
items.note: Baking soda + buttermilk make the bubbles.

items.name: Cornbread
items.note: American South. Cornmeal and baking powder.

items.name: Banana bread
items.note: Really a cake in a loaf pan.

facts: Yeast is a tiny living fungus. It eats sugar in the flour and breathes out carbon dioxide gas — the bubbles.
Kneading builds gluten: stretchy protein strands that trap the gas like a balloon.
Quick breads skip the yeast: acid + baking soda make the gas in minutes, not hours.
Bakers write recipes as percentages of the flour. 500 g flour + 350 g water = 70% water.
doIt: A basic loaf is 500 g flour, 350 g water, 10 g salt, 5 g yeast. Write each as a percentage of the flour. Then scale the recipe for 2 loaves and for half a loaf.

quiz.why: Yeast eats sugar and makes CO₂ gas.
Boiling sets the outside before the oven.
Unleavened means nothing makes it rise.

quiz.q: 500 g flour and 350 g water. What % water?

title: Shares, stocks, and options
hook: Companies sell small pieces of themselves to raise money. Knowing how that works helps you save — and understand the news.

items.name: Share (stock)
items.note: A tiny piece of a company. Own 1 of 1,000 shares → you own 0.1%.

items.name: Stock exchange
items.note: The market where shares are bought and sold. NYSE and Nasdaq are in New York.

items.name: IPO
items.note: Initial public offering: the first day a company sells shares to the public.

items.name: Market cap
items.note: Share price × number of shares = what the market says the company is worth.

items.name: Dividend
items.note: Part of the profit paid to shareholders, often every 3 months.

items.name: Index
items.note: An average of many stocks. The S&P 500 tracks 500 large US companies.

items.name: Bull market
items.note: Prices rising for a long time. (A bull attacks upward.)

items.name: Bear market
items.note: Prices down 20% or more. (A bear swipes down.)

items.name: Bond
items.note: A loan you give a company or government. Safer, lower return.

items.name: Index fund
items.note: Buys every stock in an index. Cheap and spread out.

items.name: Diversification
items.note: Don't put all your eggs in one basket. One company can fail; 500 rarely all do.

items.name: Call option
items.note: The right to BUY a share at a set price later. You bet the price goes up.

items.name: Put option
items.note: The right to SELL at a set price later. You bet it goes down — or insure against it.

facts: Over long periods the S&P 500 has grown about 10% a year on average — but some years it fell 30% or more.
Options are risky: if the price doesn't move your way by the date, the option can become worth $0.
The richest 10% of US households own about 90% of all stocks. That's one reason stock-market news often matters more to the wealthy than to workers.
Prices move because of supply and demand: more buyers than sellers pushes the price up.
doIt: On the sheet: you buy 10 shares at $50. Work out your gain if the price goes to $60, and your loss if it drops to $35. Then pick 3 companies whose products you use every day. Tonight, ask Dad to look up their prices with you. Check them again in one month.

quiz.q: You own 50 of a company's 1,000 shares. What do you own?

options: A fund that buys every stock in an index
quiz.why: It spreads money across many companies.

quiz.q: A call option pays off when the price…
quiz.why: It's the right to buy at a fixed price.

quiz.q: Which is usually safer, with lower return?
quiz.why: A bond is a loan that is paid back with interest.

title: What you can study at university
hook: Universities sort knowledge into faculties (also called schools or colleges). Knowing the map helps you see where your interests could lead.

items.name: Humanities
items.note: History, philosophy, literature, languages, religion. How people think and have lived.

items.name: Social sciences
items.note: Economics, psychology, sociology, political science, anthropology. How societies work, using data.

items.name: Fine arts
items.note: Music, painting, theater, film, architecture.

items.name: Education
items.note: How people learn; training to be a teacher.

items.name: Natural sciences
items.note: Physics, chemistry, biology, earth science. Experiments about nature.

items.name: Formal sciences
items.note: Mathematics, statistics, computer science. Proofs and logic.

items.name: Engineering
items.note: Civil (bridges), mechanical (machines), electrical, chemical, software. Using science to build.

items.name: Medicine and health
items.note: Medicine, nursing, pharmacy, dentistry, public health.

items.name: Law
items.note: How laws are made, used, and challenged in court.

items.name: Business
items.note: Accounting, finance, marketing, management.

items.name: Associate
items.note: 2 years, often at a community college.

items.name: Bachelor's (BA / BS)
items.note: 4 years. The usual first degree.

items.name: Master's (MA / MS)
items.note: 1–2 more years, more specialized.

items.name: PhD
items.note: 4–6+ years of original research. Makes you “Dr.”

items.name: MD / JD
items.note: Doctor: 4 years after college + 3–7 of residency. Lawyer: 3 years after college.

facts: Your “major” is your main subject. Most students also take classes far outside it.
Many fields cross faculties: neuroscience mixes biology and psychology; economics uses a lot of math.
Community college costs much less, and many students start there, then transfer for the last 2 years.
Public universities are funded partly by taxes so more people can attend, not just those who can pay.
doIt: On the sheet, sort the 25 subjects into their faculties. Then circle the 2 you would most want to try, and write one sentence on why.

quiz.why: It studies people using experiments and data.
Formal sciences use logic and proofs, not lab experiments.

quiz.q: How long is a bachelor's degree, usually?
quiz.why: An associate degree is the 2-year one.

quiz.q: Building bridges is which kind of engineering?
quiz.why: Civil engineers design roads, bridges, and water systems.

title: 20 famous books
hook: These books come up again and again — in school, in movies, in conversation. Knowing one line about each lets you join in, and helps you pick your next read.

items.name: The Odyssey — Homer (Greece, ~700 BCE)
items.note: A soldier's 10-year trip home from war.

items.name: Don Quixote — Cervantes (Spain, 1605)
items.note: A man reads too many hero stories and attacks windmills.

items.name: Pride and Prejudice — Jane Austen (1813)
items.note: Love, money, and first impressions in England.

items.name: Frankenstein — Mary Shelley (1818)
items.note: A scientist builds a creature, then abandons it.

items.name: Les Misérables — Victor Hugo (1862)
items.note: A poor man jailed for stealing bread tries to start over.

items.name: Crime and Punishment — Dostoevsky (1866)
items.note: A student commits a murder and is eaten by guilt.

items.name: Huckleberry Finn — Mark Twain (1884)
items.note: A boy and an escaped enslaved man, Jim, on the Mississippi.

items.name: Brave New World — Aldous Huxley (1932)
items.note: A future where people are kept happy and controlled.

items.name: Animal Farm — George Orwell (1945)
items.note: Farm animals overthrow the farmer — then the pigs take over.

items.name: 1984 — George Orwell (1949)
items.note: A government that watches everyone. “Big Brother.”

items.name: Fahrenheit 451 — Ray Bradbury (1953)
items.note: Firemen whose job is to burn books.

items.name: Lord of the Flies — William Golding (1954)
items.note: Stranded boys build — and wreck — their own society.

items.name: The Grapes of Wrath — John Steinbeck (1939)
items.note: A farm family flees the Dust Bowl and meets exploitation in California.

items.name: The Diary of Anne Frank (1947)
items.note: A Jewish girl hiding from the Nazis in Amsterdam.

items.name: Things Fall Apart — Chinua Achebe (1958)
items.note: A Nigerian village before and after colonial rule.

items.name: To Kill a Mockingbird — Harper Lee (1960)
items.note: A girl watches her father defend a Black man in the racist South.

items.name: One Hundred Years of Solitude — García Márquez (1967)
items.note: Seven generations of one family in a magical Colombian town.

items.name: Beloved — Toni Morrison (1987)
items.note: The haunting cost of slavery after escape.

items.name: The Hobbit — J.R.R. Tolkien (1937)
items.note: A quiet hobbit joins dwarves to face a dragon.

items.name: The Little Prince — Saint-Exupéry (1943)
items.note: A pilot meets a boy from a tiny planet. Short, deep.

facts: Good starters at 12: The Hobbit, Animal Farm, The Little Prince, The Diary of Anne Frank, Fahrenheit 451.
Orwell wrote both Animal Farm and 1984. Both warn about leaders who lie to keep power.
Several of these were banned in some US schools at times — usually because they made powerful people uncomfortable.
Things Fall Apart is one of the most-read African novels; Achebe wrote it partly to answer how European books pictured Africa.
doIt: On the sheet, match each book to its one-line story. Then choose ONE book you want to read next and write why. Give the sheet to Dad — he'll get the book.

quiz.q: Who wrote both Animal Farm and 1984?
In Fahrenheit 451, what do firemen do?
quiz.why: 451°F is said to be the temperature paper burns.

quiz.q: Which book is set in a Nigerian village?

pairs: A scientist builds a creature, then abandons it
The pigs take over after the revolution
A lawyer defends a Black man in the South
A hobbit, dwarves, and a dragon
A Nigerian village meets colonial rule
A family flees the Dust Bowl
Hiding from the Nazis in Amsterdam

title: How common medicines work
hook: Most medicines in a home cabinet do one of a few jobs. Knowing which is which keeps you safe — and explains why some don't help at all.

items.name: NSAIDs — ibuprofen (Advil), naproxen (Aleve), aspirin
items.note: Block an enzyme (COX) that makes pain-and-swelling signals. Lower pain, fever, and swelling. Can upset the stomach.

items.name: Acetaminophen (Tylenol)
items.note: Lowers pain and fever but not swelling. Too much damages the liver — it hides in many cold medicines, so doses add up.

items.name: Corticosteroids — prednisone, hydrocortisone cream, asthma inhalers
items.note: Turn down inflammation: rashes, asthma, bad allergies. Not the same as the “steroids” some athletes misuse.

items.name: Antihistamines — cetirizine (Zyrtec), diphenhydramine (Benadryl)
items.note: Block histamine, the chemical behind sneezing and itching. Older ones cause sleepiness.

items.name: Antibiotics — penicillin, amoxicillin
items.note: Kill bacteria. Useless against viruses like colds and flu.

items.name: Antivirals — Tamiflu, Paxlovid
items.note: Slow a specific virus from copying itself.

items.name: Vaccines
items.note: Show the body a harmless piece of a germ so it is ready next time.

items.name: Insulin
items.note: Lets cells take in sugar. People with type 1 diabetes need it to live.

items.name: Albuterol inhaler
items.note: Relaxes the muscles around the airways in an asthma attack.

items.name: Statins
items.note: Lower cholesterol to protect the heart.

items.name: Antacids
items.note: Neutralize stomach acid (a base cancels an acid).

facts: Never take any medicine without asking Dad. The right dose depends on your weight and age.
Generic drugs have the same active ingredient as the brand name, and usually cost far less.
Alexander Fleming noticed in 1928 that a mold killed bacteria — that became penicillin.
Using antibiotics when they aren't needed helps bacteria evolve resistance, so they stop working for everyone.
doIt: With Dad, take out 2 medicine boxes from the house. On the sheet, copy the active ingredient, what it treats, the dose, and one warning. Then write which family above it belongs to.

quiz.q: You have a cold (a virus). Will an antibiotic help?
Which lowers swelling as well as pain?
quiz.why: Ibuprofen is an NSAID; acetaminophen doesn't reduce swelling.
It blocks histamine, which causes sneezing and itching.

quiz.q: A generic drug compared to the brand name is…
quiz.why: Same medicine, different name and price.

title: Reading a nutrition label
hook: The front of a box is advertising. The back is the truth. Two minutes with the label tells you what you're really eating.

items.name: Serving size
items.note: Everything below is for ONE serving. A bag can hold 3 servings — eat it all and triple the numbers.

items.name: Calories
items.note: Energy. A 12-year-old needs roughly 1,800–2,400 a day, depending on activity.

items.name: Added sugars
items.note: Sugar put in during making. Kids should stay under about 25 g a day.

items.name: Sodium (salt)
items.note: Aim for under 2,300 mg a day. Chips, soups, and fast food are full of it.

items.name: Saturated fat
items.note: Mostly from meat, butter, cheese. Too much is hard on the heart.

items.name: Fiber
items.note: Keeps you full and your gut healthy. Beans, whole grains, fruit.

items.name: Protein
items.note: Builds muscle. Eggs, beans, yogurt, chicken, nuts.

items.name: Vitamins and minerals
items.note: Iron, calcium, vitamin D, potassium.

items.name: % Daily Value
items.note: 5% or less = low. 20% or more = high.

items.name: Ingredients list
items.note: Ordered by weight, biggest first. If sugar is first, it's mostly sugar.

facts: 4 grams of sugar ≈ 1 teaspoon. A 12-oz soda has about 39 g — nearly 10 teaspoons.
Sugar hides under many names: corn syrup, dextrose, cane juice, maltose.
Food companies spend billions advertising sugary foods to kids — often in poorer neighborhoods where fresh food is harder to find.
“Natural” on the front means almost nothing legally. The label on the back is regulated.
doIt: Pick 3 packaged foods from the kitchen. Fill in the table. Turn the added sugar into teaspoons (÷ 4). Which one surprised you?

quiz.q: A bag has 3 servings of 150 calories. You eat it all. How many calories?
20 g of added sugar is about how many teaspoons?
A food shows 25% of the Daily Value for sodium. That is…
The first ingredient listed is the one with…

title: Compound interest
hook: Money that earns interest, then earns interest on that interest, grows faster every year. Time matters more than the amount.

items.name: Principal
items.note: The money you start with.

items.name: Interest rate
items.note: The percent added each year. 5% of $100 = $5.

items.name: Simple interest
items.note: Interest only on the principal. $100 at 10% → $110, $120, $130…

items.name: Compound interest
items.note: Interest on the new total. $100 at 10% → $110, $121, $133.10…

items.name: Rule of 72
items.note: 72 ÷ rate = years to double. At 8%, money doubles in about 9 years.

items.name: Savings account
items.note: Safe; usually 0.5–4% a year.

items.name: Index fund
items.note: Has averaged roughly 7% a year after inflation over long periods — with bad years.

items.name: Inflation
items.note: Prices rising, about 2–3% in a normal year. Money under a mattress loses value.

items.name: Start at 15
items.note: $100 a month at 7% until 65 → about $545,000. You put in $60,000.

items.name: Start at 25
items.note: Same $100 a month → about $262,000. You put in $48,000.

items.name: Debt compounds too
items.note: A loan or credit card grows the same way — against you.

facts: The 10 years from 15 to 25 add only $12,000 of savings but more than double the result.
Compound interest helps people who already have money most — one reason wealth gaps grow over time.
Many countries and some US states now start a small savings account for every child at birth.
Formula: total = principal × (1 + rate)^years.
doIt: Fill in the table: $1,000 growing at 10% a year, compounded. Then use the Rule of 72 for 6%, 8%, and 12%.

quiz.q: Rule of 72 at 6%: years to double?

quiz.why: The same dollar buys a little less each year.

title: First aid basics
hook: Most injuries at home are small — if you know the first two minutes. And knowing when to call 911 can save a life.

items.name: Isn't breathing or won't wake up
items.note: Call first, then follow what the dispatcher says.

items.name: Has chest pain or a seizure
items.note: Clear space around them. Don't hold them down.

items.name: Is bleeding a lot
items.note: Blood soaking through cloth, or spurting.

items.name: Has a swollen face or lips after food or a sting
items.note: Severe allergy. If they have an EpiPen, help them use it.

items.name: Burn
items.note: Cool running water for 20 minutes. No ice, no butter.

items.name: Cut
items.note: Press with a clean cloth for 10 minutes without peeking. Raise it.

items.name: Nosebleed
items.note: Lean FORWARD, pinch the soft part for 10 minutes. Not back.

items.name: Sprain
items.note: Rest, Ice (in a cloth, 20 min), Compress, Elevate.

items.name: Bee sting
items.note: Scrape the stinger out sideways with a card. Ice.

items.name: Can cough or talk
items.note: Let them keep coughing. Stay with them.

items.name: Can't breathe, speak, or cough
items.note: Call 911. 5 firm back blows between the shoulder blades, then 5 abdominal thrusts. Repeat.
Emergency. Say your address first.
Poison Control, for swallowed chemicals or pills. Free, 24/7.

facts: The recovery position: on their side, top knee bent, head tilted back. Keeps the airway open for someone breathing but not awake.
After a hit to the head, watch for confusion, vomiting, or bad headache — those mean a doctor today.
In the US, 911 calls can be made from any phone, even one with no service plan.
Free CPR classes are offered by the Red Cross and many fire departments. Anyone 12+ can learn.
doIt: Find the first-aid kit in the house. List what's inside. Then write the exact words you'd say to a 911 dispatcher, starting with our address.

quiz.q: Someone choking can still cough. You…
quiz.why: Coughing is the best way to clear it.

title: 15 cheeses
hook: Every cheese starts the same way: milk, bacteria, and time. What changes is the milk, the moisture, and how long it ages.

items.name: Mozzarella
items.note: Italy. Stretchy when melted — pizza.

items.name: Ricotta
items.note: Italy. Soft and grainy, made from leftover whey. Lasagne.

items.name: Feta
items.note: Greece. Salty, crumbly, kept in brine. Sheep or goat milk.

items.name: Cream cheese
items.note: USA. Smooth and spreadable. Bagels, cheesecake.

items.name: Paneer
items.note: India. Doesn't melt, so it can be fried in curry.

items.name: Brie
items.note: France. White fuzzy rind you can eat, gooey inside.

items.name: Camembert
items.note: France. Like brie, smaller and stronger.

items.name: Cheddar
items.note: England. Sharper the longer it ages.

items.name: Gouda
items.note: Netherlands. Mild and creamy; aged gouda is crunchy.

items.name: Swiss (Emmental)
items.note: Switzerland. Bacteria make gas bubbles — the holes.

items.name: Monterey Jack
items.note: California. Mild, melts well.

items.name: Parmesan
items.note: Italy. Aged 12+ months. Grated on pasta.

items.name: Manchego
items.note: Spain. Sheep milk, nutty.

items.name: Roquefort
items.note: France. Sheep milk, blue mold veins.

items.name: Gorgonzola
items.note: Italy. Creamy blue.

facts: How cheese is made: warm milk + bacteria + rennet → it splits into curds (solid) and whey (liquid). Press the curds, salt them, age them.
Kosher cheese uses rennet made by microbes instead of from animals.
Most adults in the world digest milk sugar (lactose) poorly. Aged cheeses have almost none left, so many people can still eat them.
The blue in blue cheese is a safe mold, Penicillium — a cousin of the one that gave us penicillin.
doIt: Find 2 cheeses in the fridge. Taste a small piece of each. Fill in the table: type, milk, texture, taste in 3 words.

quiz.q: Why does Swiss cheese have holes?
quiz.why: CO₂ gas from bacteria while it ages.

quiz.q: Which cheese is kept in salty brine?
quiz.why: Brine keeps feta moist and salty.
Curds and whey, like the nursery rhyme.

quiz.q: Which cheese doesn't melt, so it can be fried?
quiz.why: Paneer holds its shape in curry.

title: How a paycheck works
hook: If a job pays $15 an hour, you don't take home $15 an hour. Here's where the rest goes — and what it pays for.

items.name: Gross pay
items.note: Hours × hourly wage. Before anything is taken out.

items.name: Net pay
items.note: What actually lands in your bank. “Take-home pay.”

items.name: Federal income tax
items.note: Pays for the military, roads, research, and more. Higher earners pay a higher rate.

items.name: State tax
items.note: Most states have one; a few (like Texas, Florida, Washington) don't.

items.name: Social Security — 6.2%
items.note: Pays retirees and disabled workers. Your employer pays another 6.2%.

items.name: Medicare — 1.45%
items.note: Health insurance for people 65+.

items.name: Minimum wage
items.note: Federal: $7.25 an hour, unchanged since 2009. Many states set it higher — over $16 in some.

items.name: Overtime
items.note: Over 40 hours a week → 1.5× pay for most hourly jobs.

items.name: Union
items.note: Workers bargaining together for pay, hours, and safety. Union workers earn more on average.

items.name: W-4
items.note: You fill it in when you start a job, so the right tax is taken out.

items.name: W-2
items.note: Your employer sends it each January: what you earned and paid in tax.

items.name: Tax refund
items.note: If too much was taken out during the year, you get it back.

facts: Social Security and Medicare together are called FICA: 7.65% from every paycheck.
Prices have risen more than 40% since 2009, so $7.25 buys much less today than when it was set.
The 40-hour week and the weekend were won by labor unions in the early 1900s.
Tipped workers can be paid as little as $2.13 an hour by federal law, if tips make up the rest.

title: 16 famous paintings
hook: These pictures show up on posters, memes, and in museums everywhere. Know who made them and why they matter.

items.name: The Birth of Venus — Botticelli (~1485)
items.note: The goddess arriving on a shell.

items.name: Mona Lisa — Leonardo da Vinci (~1503–1519)
items.note: The famous smile. In the Louvre, Paris.

items.name: The Creation of Adam — Michelangelo (1512)
items.note: Two fingers almost touching, on the Sistine Chapel ceiling.

items.name: The Night Watch — Rembrandt (1642)
items.note: A huge group portrait full of light and shadow.

items.name: Las Meninas — Velázquez (1656)
items.note: A princess, her maids, and the painter himself looking at you.

items.name: Girl with a Pearl Earring — Vermeer (~1665)
items.note: A girl turning over her shoulder.

items.name: Liberty Leading the People — Delacroix (1830)
items.note: A woman with a flag leads a revolution in Paris.

items.name: The Great Wave — Hokusai (~1831)
items.note: Japanese woodblock print; a wave towers over boats.

items.name: Water Lilies — Claude Monet (1890s–1920s)
items.note: Impressionism: blurry light on his pond.

items.name: The Starry Night — Van Gogh (1889)
items.note: Swirling sky, painted from his window at a hospital.

items.name: The Scream — Edvard Munch (1893)
items.note: A figure holding its face under a red sky.

items.name: American Gothic — Grant Wood (1930)
items.note: A farmer with a pitchfork and his daughter.

items.name: The Persistence of Memory — Dalí (1931)
items.note: Melting clocks. Surrealism: dream images.

items.name: Guernica — Picasso (1937)
items.note: Protest against the bombing of a Spanish town in the civil war.

items.name: The Two Fridas — Frida Kahlo (1939)
items.note: Two versions of herself, Mexican and European, holding hands.

items.name: Nighthawks — Edward Hopper (1942)
items.note: Lonely people in a late-night diner.

facts: Van Gogh sold almost nothing while alive. Today his paintings sell for over $100 million.
Guernica is black, white, and gray, like newspaper photos of the bombing.
For centuries, women were mostly kept out of art schools. Artists like Artemisia Gentileschi and Frida Kahlo were overlooked for a long time.
Many museums are free or pay-what-you-wish one day a week, so art isn't only for those who can pay.
doIt: On the sheet, match each painting to what it shows. Then pick one to hang in your room and write why in one sentence. Tonight, ask Dad to show you the real picture.

pairs: A swirling sky from a hospital window
Two versions of the painter holding hands

quiz.why: Picasso painted it in protest in 1937.
It has hung in the Louvre for over 200 years.

title: Knife skills
hook: Cutting well is the first skill of cooking. Done right, it's fast and safe. Only with Dad or another adult in the kitchen today.

items.name: The claw
items.note: Curl the fingertips of the holding hand under, knuckles against the blade.

items.name: A sharp knife is safer
items.note: A dull knife slips. A sharp one goes where you aim.

items.name: Steady board
items.note: Put a damp paper towel under the cutting board so it can't slide.

items.name: Never catch a falling knife
items.note: Step back and let it fall.

items.name: Never in the sink
items.note: Someone could reach into the water. Wash it, dry it, put it away.

items.name: Chef's knife
items.note: Big, for almost everything.

items.name: Paring knife
items.note: Small, for peeling and little jobs.

items.name: Serrated (bread) knife
items.note: Saw teeth, for bread and tomatoes.

items.name: Rough chop
items.note: Uneven pieces. Fine for soups.

items.name: Dice
items.note: Even cubes, so everything cooks at the same speed.

items.name: Mince
items.note: Very tiny pieces. Garlic, herbs.

items.name: Slice
items.note: Even flat pieces.

items.name: Julienne
items.note: Matchsticks. Carrots for stir-fry.

items.name: Chiffonade
items.note: Roll leaves up like a cigar, slice into ribbons. Basil.

facts: Dicing an onion: cut in half through the root, peel, make flat cuts toward the root, then down cuts, then across. The root holds it together.
Onions make you cry because cutting them releases a gas that turns into a mild acid in your eyes. A sharp knife crushes fewer cells.
Even pieces aren't about looks — small pieces burn while big ones stay raw.
Rock the chef's knife: tip stays on the board, the handle goes up and down.
doIt: With Dad in the kitchen: dice half an onion and slice a carrot, then julienne the rest of it. Check each box on the sheet when done.

items: ☐ Board on a damp towel   ☐ Claw grip the whole time
☐ Diced half an onion — were the cubes even?
☐ Sliced a carrot   ☐ Julienned the rest
☐ Washed and put away the knife (not in the sink)
What was hardest?

options: Step back and let it fall

quiz.q: Why cut pieces the same size?
quiz.why: Small ones burn while big ones stay raw.

title: Credit cards and debt
hook: A credit card is a loan with a very high interest rate. Used carefully it's handy. Used carelessly it's a trap built to make money from you.

items.name: Debit card
items.note: Spends money already in your bank account.

items.name: Credit card
items.note: Spends the bank's money. You owe it back.

items.name: Pay in full each month
items.note: Then you pay zero interest. This is the safe way.

items.name: APR
items.note: Annual interest rate. Credit cards average over 20% a year.

items.name: Minimum payment
items.note: The tiny amount they let you pay. Most of it goes to interest.

items.name: Late fee
items.note: Often $30 or more for one late payment.

items.name: Payday loan
items.note: Short loans at rates near 400% a year, often in poorer neighborhoods. Avoid.

items.name: Buy now, pay later
items.note: Splits a purchase into payments. Easy to stack up too many.

items.name: What it is
items.note: A number from 300 to 850 that says how risky lending to you seems.

items.name: What it affects
items.note: Renting an apartment, a car loan, sometimes even a job.

items.name: How to keep it high
items.note: Pay on time, owe little compared to your limit.

facts: $1,000 on a card at 24% APR, paying $25 a month: about 7 years to pay off, and about $2,000 paid in total.
24% a year is 2% a month. On $1,000 that's $20 of interest — so a $25 payment cuts only $5 off the debt.
Card companies earn the most from people who can only afford the minimum.
Store “0% for 12 months” offers often charge all the back-interest if you're one day late paying it off.
doIt: On the sheet: $1,000 balance, 2% interest a month, $25 payment. Work out 3 months. How much did the balance actually drop?

quiz.q: How do you pay zero interest on a credit card?
options: Pay the full balance every month
quiz.why: Interest only starts on unpaid balance.

title: Spices of the world
hook: Spices made food exciting — and made empires rich. Learn 16 by name, by smell, and by the food that uses them.

items.name: Cumin
items.note: Mexico, India, Middle East. Smoky. In tacos and curry.

items.name: Turmeric
items.note: India. Bright yellow, earthy. Colors curry.

items.name: Paprika
items.note: Hungary, Spain. Ground red peppers, sweet or smoked.

items.name: Cinnamon
items.note: Sri Lanka. The bark of a tree.

items.name: Nutmeg
items.note: Indonesia. A seed. Pumpkin pie.

items.name: Cloves
items.note: Indonesia. Dried flower buds. Very strong.

items.name: Black pepper
items.note: India. Once so valuable it was called black gold.

items.name: Ginger
items.note: Asia. A root, spicy-fresh. Stir-fries, cookies.

items.name: Chili / cayenne
items.note: From the Americas. The heat is a chemical, capsaicin.

items.name: Sumac
items.note: Middle East. Tangy red berries. On salads and meat.

items.name: Cardamom
items.note: India. In chai and Scandinavian buns.

items.name: Saffron
items.note: Iran. Threads from crocus flowers. The most expensive spice by weight.

items.name: Star anise
items.note: China. Licorice smell. In five-spice powder.

items.name: Za'atar
items.note: Thyme, sumac, sesame. Middle East, on bread with oil.

items.name: Garam masala
items.note: India. A warm mix added at the end of cooking.

items.name: Chili powder
items.note: USA. Chili, cumin, garlic, oregano. Chili con carne.

facts: Columbus sailed west in 1492 looking for a faster route to Asia's spices.
In 1621 the Dutch East India Company killed or enslaved most people on the Banda Islands to control the nutmeg trade.
Chili peppers came from the Americas. Before 1492, there was no chili in Indian or Thai food.
Spices lose smell over time. A jar older than about 2 years is mostly dust.
doIt: Ask Dad to pick 5 spice jars and hide the labels. Smell each one and guess. Fill in the table.

quiz.q: Which spice is the bark of a tree?
Where did chili peppers come from?
quiz.why: They spread around the world after 1492.

quiz.q: The most expensive spice by weight?
quiz.why: Each thread is picked by hand from a flower.

title: How your body fights germs
hook: Every day your immune system fights off invaders you never notice. When you do feel sick, much of what you feel is the fight itself.

items.name: Skin
items.note: The first barrier. A cut is an open door.

items.name: Mucus and tiny hairs
items.note: In your nose and lungs, trap germs so you sneeze or cough them out.

items.name: Stomach acid
items.note: Kills most germs you swallow.

items.name: Neutrophils
items.note: First to arrive. Swallow bacteria. Pus is mostly dead neutrophils.

items.name: Macrophages
items.note: “Big eaters.” Eat germs and show pieces to other cells.

items.name: B cells
items.note: Make antibodies: Y-shaped proteins that stick to one exact germ.

items.name: T cells
items.note: Kill infected cells and direct the fight.

items.name: Memory cells
items.note: Remember a germ for years — why you rarely get chickenpox twice.

items.name: Fever
items.note: Heat slows germs and speeds up immune cells.

items.name: Swelling and redness
items.note: More blood brings more soldiers to the spot.

items.name: Swollen lymph nodes
items.note: The “glands” in your neck, where immune cells gather.

items.name: Allergy
items.note: Overreacting to something harmless, like pollen or peanuts.

items.name: Autoimmune disease
items.note: Attacking your own body, like type 1 diabetes.

facts: In 1721, an enslaved African man in Boston named Onesimus taught the town about inoculation, a practice from West Africa. It saved many lives in a smallpox outbreak.
Edward Jenner made the first vaccine in 1796, using cowpox to protect against smallpox.
Vaccines wiped out smallpox completely by 1980 — the only human disease ever eradicated.
Herd immunity: when most people are immune, a germ can't spread, which protects babies and sick people who can't be vaccinated.
doIt: On the sheet, draw a germ entering through a cut. Label the 4 steps of the fight in order: barrier, first responders, antibodies, memory.

items: Draw it here (cut, germ, white blood cells):
Step 1 — barrier:
Step 2 — first responders:
Step 3 — antibodies:
Step 4 — memory:

quiz.why: B cells build antibodies for one exact germ.

quiz.q: Why do you rarely get chickenpox twice?

quiz.why: Pollen isn't dangerous; the reaction is.

quiz.q: The only human disease wiped out by vaccines?

title: A family tree of music
hook: Most popular music today grew from a few roots — many of them created by Black Americans. Learn how one style led to the next.

items.name: Classical
items.note: Europe, 1600s–1800s. Bach, Mozart, Beethoven. Orchestras, written scores.

items.name: Blues
items.note: Mississippi Delta, ~1900. Black Americans after slavery. Sad songs, 12-bar pattern.

items.name: Gospel
items.note: Black churches. Big voices, call and response.

items.name: Jazz
items.note: New Orleans, 1910s. Improvising — making it up live. Louis Armstrong.

items.name: Country
items.note: Appalachia and the South, 1920s. Fiddle, guitar — and the banjo, which came from West Africa.

items.name: Rock and roll
items.note: 1950s, from rhythm and blues. Sister Rosetta Tharpe, Chuck Berry, Little Richard.

items.name: Soul / Motown
items.note: Detroit, 1960s. Aretha Franklin, Stevie Wonder.

items.name: Reggae
items.note: Jamaica, late 1960s. Off-beat rhythm, songs about freedom. Bob Marley.

items.name: Salsa
items.note: New York's Puerto Rican and Cuban communities, 1960s–70s. Celia Cruz.

items.name: Afrobeat
items.note: Nigeria, 1970s. Fela Kuti, songs against the military government.

items.name: Hip-hop
items.note: The Bronx, New York, 1973. DJ Kool Herc looped drum breaks; rappers rhymed over them.

items.name: House / electronic
items.note: Chicago, 1980s, in Black and gay dance clubs.

items.name: K-pop
items.note: South Korea, 1990s on. Mixes pop, hip-hop, and dance.

facts: Sister Rosetta Tharpe, a Black woman playing electric guitar in the 1930s–40s, is called the godmother of rock and roll.
Early rock and roll by Black artists was often re-recorded by white singers who got the radio play and money.
Hip-hop started at block parties in one of the poorest parts of New York and became the most-streamed genre in the US.
Many genres began as music of protest: blues, reggae, Afrobeat, punk, hip-hop.
doIt: On the sheet, match each genre to where it was born. Tonight after school, play 30 seconds of 5 genres with Dad and pick a favorite.

pairs: Puerto Rican and Cuban New York

quiz.why: Musicians make it up as they play.
Enslaved Africans brought it to America.

quiz.q: Rock and roll grew mostly from…
quiz.why: R&B by Black artists in the 1940s–50s.

title: Basic tools and home repair
hook: Most small fixes need just a few tools and the right word for them. Learn them now and you'll never feel stuck when something wobbles or leaks.

items.name: Phillips screwdriver
items.note: Cross-shaped tip, for + screws. The most common.

items.name: Flathead screwdriver
items.note: Flat tip, for — screws. Also opens paint cans.

items.name: Claw hammer
items.note: Drives nails; the claw pulls them out.

items.name: Tape measure
items.note: Locks in place. The hook at the end slides a little on purpose.

items.name: Level
items.note: The bubble in the middle means perfectly flat.

items.name: Pliers
items.note: Grip, bend, and hold. Needle-nose for small spaces.

items.name: Adjustable wrench
items.note: Turns nuts and bolts of any size.

items.name: Allen key (hex key)
items.note: Little L-shaped tool for furniture you assemble yourself.

items.name: Utility knife
items.note: Opens boxes, cuts carpet. Blade retracts — always close it.

items.name: Water shut-off valve
items.note: Turns off all the water if a pipe bursts.

items.name: Breaker panel
items.note: Switches that cut power to parts of the house. A “tripped” breaker is flipped to the middle.

items.name: Plunger
items.note: Unclogs a toilet: seal it over the hole, push and pull.

items.name: WD-40
items.note: Pushes out water and loosens stuck metal. Stops squeaks.

items.name: Duct tape
items.note: Temporary fix for almost anything.

items.name: Painter's tape
items.note: Peels off clean. For marking and painting edges.

facts: Righty-tighty, lefty-loosey: turn clockwise to tighten, counter-clockwise to loosen.
Never work on anything electrical unless the breaker is off — and ask an adult first.
Many cities have free “tool libraries” where you can borrow tools instead of buying them.
The “right to repair” movement fights for people to be able to fix their own phones, cars, and tractors instead of being forced to pay the company.
doIt: Find 5 tools in the house and fill in the table. Then ask Dad to show you the water shut-off and the breaker panel. Tighten one loose thing — a cabinet handle, a chair screw.

columns: Where it is in the house

quiz.q: To loosen a screw you turn…

options: Turn off the main water valve

title: Making a budget
hook: A budget is a plan for your money before you spend it. Without one, money disappears and you don't know where.

items.name: Income
items.note: Money coming in: take-home pay.

items.name: Fixed expenses
items.note: Same every month: rent, phone, insurance.

items.name: Variable expenses
items.note: Change each month: food, gas, fun.

items.name: Needs vs. wants
items.note: Need: rent, food, transport. Want: new sneakers, streaming.

items.name: Emergency fund
items.note: 3–6 months of expenses saved, for a lost job or a big bill.

items.name: 50% needs
items.note: Housing, groceries, bills, transport.

items.name: 30% wants
items.note: Eating out, hobbies, gifts.

items.name: 20% savings
items.note: Emergency fund, retirement, paying off debt.

items.name: The 30% guideline
items.note: Rent should be no more than 30% of income.

items.name: Rent-burdened
items.note: Paying more than 30%. About half of US renters are.

items.name: Roommates
items.note: The most common way young people make rent work.

facts: Write the budget before the month starts, then check it at the end. Where did you go over?
Small daily costs add up: $6 a day on snacks is about $180 a month.
In many cities, a full-time minimum-wage job can't cover a one-bedroom apartment at 30% of income.
Pay yourself first: move savings out the day you're paid, before you can spend it.
doIt: You take home $3,000 a month. Fill in the budget so the total is exactly $3,000. Rent is $1,100. Mark each line N (need) or W (want).

quiz.q: An emergency fund should cover about…
quiz.why: Enough to get through a lost job.

title: Coffee, tea, and chocolate
hook: Three things billions of people enjoy every day. Each started in one place, spread with trade and empire, and is still grown mostly by poor farmers far away.

items.name: Origin
items.note: Ethiopia. Traded through Yemen by the 1400s.

items.name: Arabica vs. robusta
items.note: Arabica: smoother, grown high up. Robusta: stronger, more caffeine.

items.name: Biggest grower today
items.note: Brazil, about a third of the world's coffee.

items.name: One plant
items.note: Green, black, white, and oolong all come from Camellia sinensis. The difference is how long the leaves oxidize (darken).

items.name: Origin
items.note: China, thousands of years ago.

items.name: Herbal “tea”
items.note: Mint or chamomile isn't really tea — no tea leaves.

items.name: Boston Tea Party, 1773
items.note: Colonists dumped British tea into the harbor to protest taxes.

items.name: Origin
items.note: Mesoamerica. The Maya and Aztecs drank it bitter; cacao beans were used as money.

items.name: Where it grows now
items.note: About 60% comes from Ivory Coast and Ghana in West Africa.

items.name: Cocoa → chocolate
items.note: Beans ferment, dry, roast, grind. Add sugar and milk for milk chocolate.

items.name: Fair trade
items.note: A label promising farmers a minimum price and no child labor.

items.name: Child labor
items.note: About 1.5 million children work on cocoa farms in Ivory Coast and Ghana.

facts: Britain sold opium in China partly to pay for tea, which led to the Opium Wars in the 1840s.
Cocoa farmers often receive only a few cents of each dollar spent on a chocolate bar.
Caffeine is a drug. Doctors advise kids and teens to have little or none.
Tea is the most-drunk drink in the world after water.
doIt: On the sheet, answer the questions. Then look at any chocolate or coffee in the house: does it have a fair trade label? Where was it grown?

items: Where did coffee, tea, and chocolate each start?
Green tea and black tea — what's the difference?
Who grows most of the world's cocoa, and what problem does fair trade try to fix?
Something in our kitchen: name, where grown, fair trade label yes/no:

quiz.why: Brazil grows the most today; Ethiopia is the origin.

quiz.q: Green and black tea come from…
The Aztecs used cacao beans as…

title: A map of careers
hook: There are thousands of jobs. Here are 20 — what they do, how long the training takes, and roughly what they pay in the US.

items.name: Electrician
items.note: Wires buildings. 4–5 year paid apprenticeship. ~$61k.

items.name: Plumber
items.note: Water and gas pipes. Paid apprenticeship. ~$61k.

items.name: Wind turbine technician
items.note: Fixes turbines. Certificate. One of the fastest-growing jobs. ~$61k.

items.name: Firefighter
items.note: Fire and medical calls. Academy of a few months. ~$57k.

items.name: Home health aide
items.note: Cares for elderly and disabled people at home. Weeks of training. ~$33k.

items.name: Truck driver
items.note: Moves goods. A few weeks for a license. ~$54k.

items.name: Registered nurse
items.note: Cares for patients. 2–4 years. ~$86k.

items.name: Dental hygienist
items.note: Cleans teeth. 2–3 years. ~$87k.

items.name: Teacher
items.note: 4–5 years. ~$65k.

items.name: Accountant
items.note: Tracks money for companies. 4 years. ~$79k.

items.name: Software developer
items.note: Builds apps. 4 years or self-taught. ~$130k.

items.name: Civil engineer
items.note: Designs bridges, roads, water systems. 4 years. ~$95k.

items.name: Social worker
items.note: Helps families in crisis. 4–6 years. ~$58k.

items.name: Graphic designer
items.note: Logos, ads, websites. 4 years. ~$58k.

items.name: Architect
items.note: Designs buildings. 5–7 years + license. ~$93k.

items.name: Physical therapist
items.note: Helps people move after injury. ~7 years. ~$99k.

items.name: Pharmacist
items.note: Medicines expert. 6–8 years. ~$135k.

items.name: Lawyer
items.note: 7 years (college + law school). ~$145k.

items.name: Airline pilot
items.note: Years of training and 1,500 flight hours. ~$220k.

items.name: Doctor
items.note: 11–15 years after high school. $230k and up.

facts: These are middle (median) pays — half earn more, half less, and it varies a lot by city.
Home health aides do some of the most essential work and are among the lowest paid. Many are immigrant women.
Trade apprenticeships pay you while you learn, with no college debt.
Most people change careers more than once. What you study isn't a life sentence.
doIt: On the sheet, list your top 3 jobs from the list (or others). For each: what draws you, and how many years of training it takes.

quiz.q: Which job has a paid apprenticeship?
Roughly how long to become a doctor after high school?

quiz.why: It's the middle value — like Day 39!

title: Sleep and your brain
hook: Sleep isn't wasted time. It's when your brain files what you learned and your body grows. Teens need more than adults — and their clocks run later.

items.name: Ages 6–12
items.note: 9–12 hours a night.

items.name: Ages 13–18
items.note: 8–10 hours a night.

items.name: Adults
items.note: 7+ hours.

items.name: Cycles
items.note: About 90 minutes each, 4–6 a night.

items.name: Light sleep
items.note: Easy to wake. Heart and breathing slow.

items.name: Deep sleep
items.note: Body repairs and grows; growth hormone is released.

items.name: REM sleep
items.note: Eyes move, dreams happen. Brain stores memories and skills.

items.name: Circadian rhythm
items.note: Your 24-hour body clock, set mostly by daylight.

items.name: Melatonin
items.note: Hormone that rises at night and makes you sleepy.

items.name: Teen shift
items.note: At puberty the clock moves about 2 hours later. Not laziness — biology.

items.name: Screens at night
items.note: Bright light and alerts delay melatonin and keep the brain busy.

items.name: Caffeine
items.note: Half of it is still in your body 5 hours later.

items.name: Changing bedtime a lot
items.note: Weekends that shift 3 hours feel like jet lag on Monday.

facts: Students remember more of what they studied if they sleep on it.
Doctors recommend middle and high schools start no earlier than 8:30 AM because of the teen body clock.
Morning sunlight helps set your clock so you get sleepy at night.
Staying up 18+ hours slows reaction time about as much as being legally drunk, studies show.
doIt: Fill in your last 3 nights: bedtime, wake time, total hours. Did you hit 8–10? What is one thing you could change?

quiz.q: How much sleep does a 13-year-old need?
Bed at 10:30 PM, up at 7:30 AM. Hours?

title: Inventions that changed the world
hook: A handful of inventions reshaped how everyone lives. Many had more than one inventor, in more than one place.

items.name: Writing — ~3200 BCE
items.note: Cuneiform in Mesopotamia (Iraq). History begins.

items.name: The wheel — ~3500 BCE
items.note: Mesopotamia. First for pottery, then carts.

items.name: Paper — ~105 CE
items.note: China, credited to Cai Lun.

items.name: Compass — ~1000s
items.note: China. Made long sea voyages possible.

items.name: Printing press — ~1440
items.note: Gutenberg, Germany. Korea printed with metal type earlier, in 1377.

items.name: Telescope — 1608
items.note: Netherlands. Galileo used it to see Jupiter's moons.

items.name: Steam engine — 1769
items.note: James Watt's improved engine powered the Industrial Revolution.

items.name: Vaccine — 1796
items.note: Edward Jenner, against smallpox.

items.name: Telephone — 1876
items.note: Alexander Graham Bell (others were close behind).

items.name: Light bulb — 1879
items.note: Edison's lasted long enough to sell; many inventors worked on it.

items.name: Airplane — 1903
items.note: The Wright brothers, 12 seconds in the air.

items.name: Penicillin — 1928
items.note: Alexander Fleming. The first antibiotic.

items.name: Transistor — 1947
items.note: Tiny switch inside every computer chip.

items.name: World Wide Web — 1989
items.note: Tim Berners-Lee — who chose not to patent it, so it was free for all.

items.name: Smartphone — 2007
items.note: The iPhone put a computer in every pocket.

facts: The printing press made books cheap, so ordinary people could read the Bible, science, and news for themselves.
Katherine Johnson and other Black women mathematicians did calculations that got NASA astronauts to orbit and back.
The jet engine, GPS, and the internet all started as government-funded research.
Most inventions build on earlier ones — the telephone needed the telegraph, which needed batteries.
doIt: On the sheet, match each invention to its date. Then pick the one you think changed the most lives and write why.

quiz.q: Who invented the World Wide Web and made it free?

title: Doing laundry
hook: Every adult needs to do this. Twenty minutes now saves shrunken sweaters and pink socks later.

items.name: Empty pockets
items.note: Tissues explode into lint; pens stain everything.

items.name: Sort
items.note: Whites, darks, colors. Towels alone — they shed.

items.name: Zip zippers, unbutton buttons
items.note: Zippers snag; buttons pop.

items.name: Read the care label
items.note: Small symbols inside the collar or side seam.

items.name: Tub
items.note: Washing. A number or dots inside = max temperature.

items.name: Hand in the tub
items.note: Hand wash only.

items.name: Triangle
items.note: Bleach. Crossed out = no bleach.

items.name: Square with a circle
items.note: Tumble dryer. One dot = low heat, three = high.

items.name: Iron
items.note: Dots for heat level.

items.name: Circle alone
items.note: Dry clean. Any symbol with an X = don't.

items.name: Cold water
items.note: Fine for most loads. Saves energy and colors.

items.name: Detergent
items.note: Follow the cap line. More soap doesn't mean cleaner.

items.name: Don't overfill
items.note: Clothes need room to move.

items.name: Clean the lint filter
items.note: Every dryer load. A clogged filter can start a fire.

facts: About 90% of a washer's energy goes to heating the water. Washing cold cuts that almost to zero.
Hang-drying makes clothes last longer and uses no electricity.
One red sock in a white load can turn everything pink — that's why you sort.
Many families without a machine spend hours a week at laundromats. A washer at home saves real time.
doIt: Do one full load with Dad: sort, read 3 labels, choose the setting, add detergent, start it. Put it in the dryer or hang it after. Fill in the table.

quiz.q: A triangle with an X means…
What should you clean after every dryer load?
Most of a washer's energy goes to…
quiz.why: So cold water saves the most.

title: How insurance works
hook: Insurance means many people pay a little so that no one person is crushed by a huge cost. Here are the words you'll see on every bill.

items.name: Risk pooling
items.note: 1,000 people each pay $500. One has a $100,000 accident — the pool covers it.

items.name: Premium
items.note: What you pay every month to be covered.

items.name: Deductible
items.note: What you pay yourself each year before insurance starts paying.

items.name: Copay
items.note: A fixed fee per visit, like $25 to see a doctor.

items.name: Coinsurance
items.note: Your percent after the deductible, like 20%.

items.name: Out-of-pocket maximum
items.note: The most you'll pay in a year. After that, insurance pays 100%.

items.name: In-network
items.note: Doctors your plan has a deal with. Out-of-network costs much more.

items.name: Health
items.note: Doctors, hospitals, medicine.

items.name: Car
items.note: Required in almost every state, to pay for damage you cause.

items.name: Renters / homeowners
items.note: Fire, theft, flood (sometimes).

items.name: Life
items.note: Pays your family if you die.

items.name: Medicare
items.note: For people 65+. Paid for from every paycheck.

items.name: Medicaid / CHIP
items.note: For people and children with low incomes.

facts: About 26 million people in the US have no health insurance.
Medical bills are one of the biggest causes of debt in the US.
Almost every other rich country covers everyone's health care, paid through taxes.
A higher deductible usually means a lower premium — you're taking more of the risk yourself.
doIt: On the sheet: your plan has a $1,000 deductible and 20% coinsurance. A hospital bill is $5,000. Work out what you pay and what insurance pays.

items: First, you pay the deductible: $
What's left of the bill after the deductible: $
Your 20% of what's left: $
Total you pay: $          Insurance pays: $
In one sentence: why do people pay for insurance even in years they don't get sick?

quiz.q: The monthly payment for insurance is the…
quiz.why: Paid whether or not you use it.
You haven't reached the deductible yet.

title: Rice and grains
hook: Rice feeds more than half the people on Earth. Each grain — rice, wheat, corn, quinoa — has a home and dishes built around it.

items.name: Basmati
items.note: India and Pakistan. Long, fluffy, separate grains. Biryani.

items.name: Jasmine
items.note: Thailand. Long, fragrant, a little sticky.

items.name: Arborio
items.note: Italy. Short and starchy — makes risotto creamy.

items.name: Sushi rice
items.note: Japan. Short and sticky, so it holds together.

items.name: Brown rice
items.note: Any rice with the bran left on. More fiber, cooks longer.

items.name: Wild rice
items.note: Not really rice — a grass seed. Ojibwe people of the Great Lakes call it manoomin.

items.name: Bulgur
items.note: Cracked wheat. Tabbouleh salad.

items.name: Couscous
items.note: North Africa. Tiny balls of semolina — really a pasta.

items.name: Farro
items.note: Ancient Italian wheat. Chewy.

items.name: Barley
items.note: Soups and beer.

items.name: Oats
items.note: Oatmeal. Lots of fiber.

items.name: Corn (maize)
items.note: Grown from a wild grass in Mexico about 9,000 years ago. Tortillas, polenta.

items.name: Quinoa
items.note: Andes mountains. A seed with complete protein.

items.name: Teff
items.note: Ethiopia. Tiny grain for injera (Extra 2!).

items.name: Millet
items.note: Africa and India. Grows in dry, hot places.

facts: Basic rice: rinse, then about 1 cup rice to 1½–2 cups water. Boil, cover, lowest heat for 15–18 minutes. Don't lift the lid.
Whole grains keep the bran and germ: more fiber and vitamins than white versions.
Rice farming needs lots of water, so droughts from climate change threaten food for billions.
Corn, potatoes, and tomatoes all came from Indigenous farmers in the Americas.
doIt: Check the kitchen for grains. Fill in the table. Then, with Dad, cook one cup of rice using the basic method.

title: How US elections work
hook: In 6 years you can vote. Here's how it works — and how the right to vote was won, and still gets fought over.

items.name: President
items.note: 4-year term, max 2 terms.

items.name: House of Representatives
items.note: 435 members. All elected every 2 years. Bigger states get more.

items.name: Senate
items.note: 100 members, 2 per state. 6-year terms.

items.name: Election Day
items.note: The Tuesday after the first Monday in November.

items.name: Register
items.note: Sign up to vote. Some states do it automatically or on Election Day.

items.name: Primary
items.note: Each party picks its candidate.

items.name: General election
items.note: Candidates from all parties face off.

items.name: Mail / absentee ballot
items.note: Vote from home. About 4 in 10 voters did in 2020.

items.name: 538 electors
items.note: Each state gets as many as its House + Senate seats. DC gets 3.

items.name: 270 to win
items.note: Most states give all their electors to whoever wins the state.

items.name: Popular vote
items.note: Total votes nationwide. A candidate can win it and still lose — it happened in 2000 and 2016.

items.name: 15th Amendment, 1870
items.note: Black men can vote — on paper. Southern states blocked them for 90 years.

items.name: 19th Amendment, 1920
items.note: Women win the vote.

items.name: Voting Rights Act, 1965
items.note: After the Selma marches. Banned literacy tests and racist rules.

items.name: 26th Amendment, 1971
items.note: Voting age lowered from 21 to 18.

facts: In 2013 the Supreme Court (Shelby County v. Holder) struck down a key part of the Voting Rights Act; several states then passed stricter voting rules.
Gerrymandering: drawing district lines to give one party an unfair advantage.
Turnout in 2020 was about 66% of eligible voters — the highest in over 100 years.
Local elections — mayor, school board — decide a lot about daily life, and often only 1 in 5 people vote in them.
doIt: On the sheet, put the steps of an election in order, then answer the 3 questions.

items: Put in order: general election · register · primary · inauguration · counting:
How many electoral votes to win the presidency?
Which amendment let women vote, and when?
What did the Voting Rights Act of 1965 ban?
In what year will you be able to vote?

quiz.q: How long is a senator's term?

quiz.why: Then the winners meet in November.

title: Mental health basics
hook: Your mind can get sick or hurt just like your body — and it can get better with help. Knowing the words makes it easier to ask.

items.name: Stress
items.note: Pressure before a test or game. Short, and can help you focus.

items.name: Sadness
items.note: After a loss or disappointment. Fades with time and support.

items.name: Anger
items.note: A signal something feels unfair. What you do with it matters.

items.name: Anxiety
items.note: Worry that won't switch off, racing heart, avoiding things.

items.name: Depression
items.note: Sad, empty, or numb most days for 2+ weeks; losing interest in things you liked.

items.name: Panic attack
items.note: Sudden fear with pounding heart and fast breathing. Scary, not dangerous, passes in minutes.

items.name: ADHD
items.note: A brain difference with focus and restlessness. Common and treatable.

items.name: A trusted adult
items.note: Dad, a relative, a teacher. Always the first step.

items.name: Counselor / therapist
items.note: Trained to talk through problems and teach skills.

items.name: Psychologist
items.note: Therapy and testing. Has a PhD or PsyD.

items.name: Psychiatrist
items.note: A medical doctor who can also prescribe medicine.
Call or text, any time, free — the Suicide & Crisis Lifeline.

items.name: Sleep, food, movement
items.note: The basics change mood more than people expect.

items.name: Time outside and with people
items.note: Even 20 minutes.

items.name: Box breathing
items.note: In 4 seconds, hold 4, out 4, hold 4. Repeat 4 times.

facts: About 1 in 5 young people has a mental health condition in a given year. It's common, not a weakness.
Asking for help is a skill, like first aid — for yourself and for friends.
In many places there aren't enough counselors, especially in poorer and rural areas.
If a friend says they want to hurt themselves, tell an adult right away, even if they asked you not to.
doIt: Do box breathing for 2 minutes. Then on the sheet write 3 things that help you calm down and 2 adults you could talk to. This sheet is private — you choose whether to show it.

items: Box breathing — how did you feel before and after?
Three things that help me calm down:
Two adults I could talk to:
One thing I could say to a friend who seems down:

quiz.q: Sad most days for over 2 weeks may be…
quiz.why: That's the sign to get help.

title: 15 classic films
hook: These movies shaped how stories are told on screen. Knowing them makes references click — and gives you a list for family movie nights.

items.name: Modern Times (1936)
items.note: Charlie Chaplin, a factory worker swallowed by machines. Silent comedy about workers.

items.name: The Wizard of Oz (1939)
items.note: A girl swept to a magical land. Early color.

items.name: Casablanca (1942)
items.note: Love and sacrifice during World War II.

items.name: It's a Wonderful Life (1946)
items.note: A man sees what his town would be without him.

items.name: Singin' in the Rain (1952)
items.note: Musical about Hollywood switching to sound.

items.name: Seven Samurai (1954)
items.note: Japan, Akira Kurosawa. Villagers hire warriors to protect them.

items.name: Star Wars (1977)
items.note: A farm boy joins a rebellion against an empire.

items.name: E.T. (1982)
items.note: A boy hides a stranded alien.

items.name: Back to the Future (1985)
items.note: A teen time-travels to when his parents were teens.

items.name: Spirited Away (2001)
items.note: Japan, Miyazaki. A girl works in a spirit bathhouse to save her parents.

items.name: Toy Story (1995)
items.note: The first feature film made fully by computer.

items.name: WALL-E (2008)
items.note: A robot cleaning up an Earth buried in trash.

items.name: Hidden Figures (2016)
items.note: The Black women mathematicians behind NASA's space race.

items.name: Coco (2017)
items.note: A Mexican boy and the Day of the Dead.

items.name: Spider-Man: Into the Spider-Verse (2018)
items.note: Miles Morales becomes Spider-Man; comic-book animation.

facts: Movies were silent until 1927; then sound changed everything (that's Singin' in the Rain).
Star Wars borrowed ideas from Seven Samurai and other Kurosawa films.
For decades, Hollywood rarely put Black, Latino, or Asian characters at the center. Films like Hidden Figures, Coco, and Spider-Verse helped change that.
Modern Times was a comedy — and also a protest against bosses speeding up factory lines.
doIt: On the sheet, match each film to its story. Circle one for family movie night this weekend and give the sheet to Dad.

pairs: A girl swept to a magical land
A farm boy joins a rebellion
A teen meets his parents as teens
A girl in a spirit bathhouse
A boy and the Day of the Dead

title: Cook a full meal
hook: Final extra: put it all together. Pasta (Extra 1), knife skills (Extra 13), spices (Extra 15), and a label check (Extra 7) — lunch for the family.

items.name: Pasta with tomato sauce
items.note: Penne or spaghetti. The sauce: olive oil, garlic, a can of tomatoes, salt, basil.

items.name: Chopped salad
items.note: Cucumber, tomato, pepper — diced even. Olive oil, lemon, salt.

items.name: 0 min
items.note: Big pot of salted water on to boil. Wash vegetables.

items.name: 5 min
items.note: Mince 2 garlic cloves. Warm oil in a pan on medium; cook garlic 1 minute — don't let it brown.

items.name: 7 min
items.note: Add tomatoes and a pinch of salt. Simmer low 15 minutes, stirring now and then.

items.name: 10 min
items.note: Pasta into the boiling water. Set a timer for the box time minus 1 minute.

items.name: 12 min
items.note: Dice the salad. Dress it just before serving.

items.name: ~22 min
items.note: Taste the pasta — al dente? Save a cup of pasta water, then drain.

items.name: 24 min
items.note: Toss pasta in the sauce with a splash of pasta water. Tear basil on top.

items.name: Dad nearby
items.note: Stove and knives only with an adult home.

items.name: Pot handles turned in
items.note: So nobody knocks them.

items.name: Clean as you go
items.note: Wash the board and knife while the sauce simmers.

items.name: Serve and clear
items.note: The cook decides the plate. Everyone helps clean up.

facts: Salt the pasta water well — it's the only chance to season the pasta itself.
Starchy pasta water makes the sauce cling. That's the cup you saved.
Cooking at home is usually far cheaper and healthier than takeout.
Being able to feed yourself and others is one of the most useful life skills there is.
doIt: Plan it on the sheet first: shopping check, timeline, who you'll serve. Then cook it with Dad home. Write what you'd change next time.
